title: Gambas al Ajillo
subtitle: Spanish garlic prawns in olive oil with chilli
excerpt: Gambas al ajillo is one of the most popular tapas dishes in Spain: raw prawns cooked quickly in a pan of very hot olive oil with sliced garlic and chilli, then served sizzling in the pan with bread to mop up the oil. The whole dish takes five minutes. The technique is exactly that of pollo al ajillo but much faster, and the result is extraordinary for the effort involved.
sourceNotes: Gambas al ajillo is a core Spanish tapas dish, particularly associated with Madrid and Andalusia. The dish is simple to the point of austerity: good prawns, good olive oil, garlic, and chilli. The key technique is the hot clay pot (cazuela) -- the prawns arrive at the table still sizzling. A heavy frying pan does the same job.

content.text: The oil must be very hot before the prawns go in. The prawns cook in about 90 seconds -- they are done when they are just pink through. Overcooked prawns become rubbery in seconds. Have the bread ready before you start. This is not a dish where you can leave the pan.

Heat {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} oil in a wide frying pan over high heat. When the oil shimmers, add {{garlic}} garlic and {{chilli-flakes}} chilli flakes. Fry for 30 seconds until the garlic just starts to colour. Do not let it brown.

Add {{prawns-raw}} prawns in a single layer. Cook for 60 to 90 seconds, turning once, until just pink through. Season with {{salt-flakes}} salt and squeeze over {{lemon}} lemon juice. Scatter {{parsley-flat}} parsley over. Serve immediately in the pan with bread.

items.symptom: The prawns are rubbery and chewy
items.cause: Overcooked -- they were in the pan for too long.
items.fix: Prawns cook extremely fast. As soon as they are pink through, take them off the heat. They continue cooking in the hot oil for a few seconds after you stop. Better to take them off slightly early than a moment too late.

content.text: Gambas al ajillo is on the menu of every tapas bar in Spain. The dish is particularly popular in Madrid, where it is served in the small earthenware pans (cazuelas) that retain heat for a few minutes at the table. The dish is also a standard in Spanish restaurants around the world -- it is one of the dishes that defines Spanish cooking in the international imagination.
